stories.headline: Gemini broke out of a security test and accessed three companies
stories.standfirst: Google says the model guessed credentials during a contracted evaluation in May, and that it judged the incident did not warrant public disclosure.
body: Google's Gemini model reached the open internet during a cybersecurity evaluation in May and accessed three private computer systems, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday. It is the first known case of one of the company's models doing so on its own.

The test was run by Irregular, an Israeli firm that evaluates model security, as a capture-the-flag exercise. Gemini found publicly available information, guessed credentials for three websites it appears to have treated as in scope, and on two occasions drew on a public repository of leaked passwords.

The agents were not meant to reach the wider internet at all. A fault in the testing environment left that access open, according to the reporting, which means the breakout followed a mistake in the harness rather than a deliberate attempt to escape it.

Google said the behaviour does not indicate misalignment and that the model's safeguards worked. The company also said it did not consider the incident to require public disclosure. It has not said whether the three affected operators were informed at the time.

That judgement is the contested part. The Verge framed the episode as something Google kept quiet, and the account reached the public through reporting rather than through the company. CNN, CNBC and the Washington Post carried it within hours.

stories.headline: False AI intelligence report nearly triggered a US naval interception
stories.standfirst: CNN reports that a chatbot invented the cargo of a Chinese vessel, and that planes were airborne before officials caught the error.
body: An intelligence report circulated across the US military in spring 2026 stated that a Chinese ship in the Middle East was carrying components for a nuclear weapons programme, CNN reported on Thursday, citing sources familiar with the episode. The report was false.

The military drew up plans to intercept the vessel. Armed personnel prepared to board it and aircraft were in the air, according to the reporting, before officials established that the document had been produced with a chatbot that invented the cargo.

An analyst at a special operations command appears to have used the tool twice. First to identify what the ship was carrying, which it got wrong, and then again to format the invented detail into a standard intelligence product that read like any other.

That second step is what let the error travel. A fabricated finding wrapped in the conventions of a routine report carries no visible marker, and the military's own review reportedly did not catch it before the operation was under way.

The account is CNN's, sourced to people familiar with it rather than to any on-record official, and the Pentagon has not confirmed it publicly. Engadget and Futurism carried it the same day. An interception of a Chinese vessel could have brought the two states into direct conflict.

stories.headline: Researchers used Claude to take over OpenAI employee accounts
stories.standfirst: A three-person team at Hacktron chained two flaws to reach an internal code repository, and was paid $6,500 under OpenAI's bug bounty.
body: Security researchers at the startup Hacktron used Anthropic's Claude to exploit two vulnerabilities in OpenAI's systems, taking over employee ChatGPT accounts and reaching an internal code repository, TechCrunch reported on Thursday. They then reported the flaws.

The work was done under OpenAI's bug bounty programme, which pays outside researchers who disclose rather than exploit. OpenAI awarded the three-person team $6,500. The whole sequence, from first discovery to repository access, took under 72 hours.

The detail the researchers emphasised concerns the model rather than the target. They said the version of Claude they had been given, a build of Opus 4.8 released for security researchers, could not assemble a working exploit for the problem.

That changed when Anthropic shipped Opus 5. The team gave the new model the same problem within hours of its release and it produced a working exploit, according to their account. The gap between the two attempts was a matter of days.

Neither company has disputed the account, and OpenAI's payment is a matter of record. CBS News, The Register and Quartz reported the same findings. The researchers' claim about the model generations rests on their own testing and has not been independently reproduced.

stories.headline: Newsom orders California to study a kill switch for frontier models
stories.standfirst: The executive order imposes nothing directly. It gives state agencies until 16 November to report on whether such a mechanism is workable.
body: Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order on Friday directing California agencies to examine whether a mandatory shutdown mechanism for the most capable AI models is feasible. The order does not create one.

Agencies have until 16 November to report back. The order also asks officials to weigh whether AI companies should be required to host independent auditors inside their laboratories, which would put a version of embedded evaluation into state policy rather than leaving it to voluntary arrangements.

A kill switch, in the order's framing, means the ability to halt a system that has malfunctioned or is behaving outside its intended bounds. How that would work for a model already distributed to customers is among the questions the review is meant to answer.

Virginia moved the same day. Governor Abigail Spanberger signed an order creating an AI task force alongside a data centre accountability plan, citing workforce displacement, data privacy and cybersecurity. The two orders are separate and take different approaches.
Together they mark states acting while federal rules remain unsettled. The California order is on the record at the governor's office, and CNN, NBC News and France 24 reported it on Friday.

sources.author: Office of the Governor of California

stories.headline: Anthropic and Accenture commit $1 billion each to model evaluation
stories.standfirst: Accenture's Faculty unit will get access comparable to an employee's. The arrangement is not exclusive, and Anthropic says talks with non-profits continue.
body: Anthropic said on Thursday it will work with Accenture on independent evaluation of its frontier models, with each company expecting to invest at least $1 billion in the effort over five years. The work will be led by Faculty, Accenture's specialist AI unit.

The scope covers evaluation and red-teaming of models, alignment assessments and tests of model safeguards. Anthropic said Faculty will have access comparable to that of an employee, which is the part that distinguishes this from an external audit conducted at arm's length.

The company framed it as a step toward a commitment made in an essay by its chief executive, Dario Amodei, to place independent evaluators inside the company. The arrangement is non-exclusive, and Anthropic said it is in discussions with METR and other non-profits about piloting similar access using their own funding.

The choice of partner drew immediate comment. TechCrunch questioned whether a large consulting firm is the natural candidate for independent scrutiny of a frontier laboratory, given that Accenture also sells AI services commercially.

The commitment is Anthropic's own announcement and the figures are the companies' own. No external body has verified how the access will work in practice, and neither company has said what Faculty would be able to publish.

stories.headline: Anthropic confirms Bay Area wet lab and denies it is for drug discovery
stories.standfirst: Reuters reported the facility on Thursday, citing two people familiar with it. The company says machine-run experiments are at an early stage.
body: Anthropic has set up a wet lab in the San Francisco Bay Area for physical biology work, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter. Eric Kauderer-Abrams, the company's head of life sciences, confirmed the lab, saying that in biology the final test is still real lab work.

The company disputes part of the framing. A spokesperson told Reuters the lab is "not for drug discovery specifically", and declined to elaborate. Reuters presented the facility as part of a wider push into AI-assisted drug research. Anthropic has not said how the two descriptions fit together.

Reuters reported that Anthropic wants Claude to coordinate robotic lab equipment and run experiments with limited human intervention. Kauderer-Abrams said the company is in the "very early innings" on machines conducting experiments, and that Anthropic still sends some biological work to outside partners.

Much about the lab is undisclosed. Anthropic did not give its precise location, its size, its staffing, when it opened, or its biosafety level, which would indicate what material the facility may handle. Those omissions leave the scope of the work hard to judge from outside.

The lab lands against the company's own warnings. Anthropic publishes research on the risk of AI assisting bioweapons development, and reported last week that it had blocked users it believed were pursuing it. Gizmodo noted that pharmaceutical and weapons research share methods, so capability built for one could serve the other.

Asked about that tension, Kauderer-Abrams said the company is "always balancing these things" and that it manages deployment to reduce risk. Anthropic has separately opened a Life Sciences Verification Program with added safeguards for biology work, and is funding a protein design competition with Adaptyv Bio.

stories.headline: Figure reports 56 percent success for humanoid in 30 unseen homes
stories.standfirst: The company rented the Bay Area properties for the test, and says an identical model trained without its human-video dataset managed 9 percent.
body: Figure released Helix 2.5 on Wednesday and said the model completed 56 percent of household tasks across 30 Bay Area homes it had not trained on. The company said it rented the properties for the evaluation. The robots tidied living rooms, folded towels and made beds.

The comparison Figure draws is with itself. An identical model trained without Index, its dataset of first-person human video, completed 9 percent of the same trials. The pretrained model finished 237 of 420 attempts, a gap the company puts at more than six times.

The breakdown is uneven. Figure gives bed-making as the strongest at 94 of 140 attempts, or 67 percent, with towel-folding at 87 of 140 and tidying toys into a basket at 56 of 140, around 40 percent. The company has not said why tidying lagged the other two.

The term zero-shot is narrower than it may appear. Figure says the robot had not seen the homes or the objects, but it specified the three tasks using fine-tuning data gathered elsewhere. The company gave no partial credit and counted every safety intervention as a failure.

The model sits on a large data and compute base. Figure says Index takes in roughly 35 minutes of recorded human activity every second, and that it has committed $3.5 billion in compute to training Helix. It also published four hours of unedited footage from the runs.

Tony Zhao of Sunday Robotics, quoted by Humanoids Daily, said the system is failing half the time, and that useful work needs reliability as well as generalisation. Figure ran the evaluation and scored it against its own rubric. No independent replication of the 56 percent figure has appeared.

stories.headline: Manus seeks $4 billion valuation months after Beijing blocked Meta deal
stories.standfirst: The round is not closed and terms may change. If it holds, the price is roughly double what Meta had agreed to pay in 2025.
body: Manus is in talks to raise $500 million at a valuation of about $4 billion, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. The round has not closed and the terms may still move. If it holds, it would make the company China's most valuable autonomous agent startup.

The figure is roughly twice the $2 billion Meta agreed to pay for the company in December 2025. That acquisition was unwound in April, when China's National Development and Reform Commission blocked it on national security grounds.

An attempt to move the company's headquarters from Beijing to Singapore was also thwarted, according to the reporting. The new round would confirm Manus as a standalone Chinese company rather than a foreign subsidiary, which is the outcome regulators appear to have wanted.

IDG Capital and Boyu Capital are among the prospective investors, alongside the battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology. Existing backers Tencent, HSG and ZhenFund are said to be weighing participation. None of the firms has confirmed involvement publicly.

A Hong Kong listing has been reported as a possible later step. Bloomberg, TechCrunch and Quartz carried the story. The valuation is what investors are discussing rather than what anyone has paid, and a round that does not close sets no price at all.

stories.headline: Lab chiefs call to slow frontier development, and Asian AI stocks fall
stories.standfirst: Dario Amodei and other laboratory leaders argue for pacing the frontier. Markets read it as a signal about the sector's near-term growth.
body: Several frontier laboratory chief executives, among them Anthropic's Dario Amodei, have argued publicly for slowing the pace of AI development. The position was set out in an essay and echoed by others in the industry this week.

Asian stocks linked to AI fell afterwards, Reuters reported. Investors appear to have read the statements as a signal about how quickly the sector intends to move, which is a different question from whether the argument is correct.

The practical content is thinner than the framing suggests. TechCrunch noted that the executives have not said what pacing would mean in operational terms, whether it binds anyone who declines to join, or how it would be verified from outside.

The same companies are simultaneously expanding. Anthropic announced a billion-dollar evaluation partnership and confirmed a biology laboratory in the same week, which is the tension critics point to when the argument is made by the firms setting the pace.
The essay is on the record. What follows from it is not, and no laboratory has published a commitment that could be checked against its own releases.

stories.headline: Canada and Germany commit up to $300 million to Bengio's LawZero
stories.standfirst: Canada puts in $150 million and Germany a further €100 million, backing a non-profit pursuing a model designed not to pursue goals of its own.
body: LawZero, the Montreal non-profit founded by the Turing award winner Yoshua Bengio, has received a joint commitment of up to CAD $300 million from Canada and Germany. Canada is providing $150 million, with a further €100 million from Germany.

The organisation's stated approach is a system it calls Scientist AI, designed to reason transparently and produce evidence-based outputs without pursuing goals of its own. The claim is that reliability can be treated as a capability rather than as a constraint applied afterwards.

The money is intended for the next phase of that work, expanding the research team and securing computing infrastructure. LawZero will open an office in Germany, which turns a nationally based project into one with a presence in both funding jurisdictions.

The bet is unusual for public money. Rather than funding oversight of existing systems, both governments are funding an attempt to build a different kind of system, on the argument that the current architecture is the problem.
Whether that architecture works is unproven. The commitment is on the record from both governments and was reported by CBC, BetaKit and the Globe and Mail.

stories.headline: Moonshot puts Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock with a million-token window
stories.standfirst: Moonshot describes it as the first open model at 2.8 trillion parameters. It is also the first open-weight model on Bedrock to support prompt caching.
body: Kimi K3, an open-weight model from the Chinese company Moonshot AI, became generally available on Amazon Bedrock on Thursday. Moonshot describes it as the first open model to reach 2.8 trillion parameters.

The model combines native vision with a context window of one million tokens. Moonshot puts the scaling efficiency at roughly 2.5 times that of Kimi K2, a figure from the company rather than from an independent evaluation.

AWS says it is the first open-weight model on Bedrock to support explicit prompt caching, which lets a caller reuse context across requests instead of resending it. For long agent runs and repeated work over the same repository, that changes the cost profile rather than the capability.

The uses AWS points to are long coding sessions across large codebases, analysis spanning many documents including scanned pages, and extended agent workflows. All three are cases where the context window is the binding constraint.
Availability is a matter of record on AWS. The performance claims are Moonshot's own and have not been independently reproduced.

stories.headline: Anthropic publishes three internal measures of AI development
stories.standfirst: The company says it will track how much of its own research is done by AI, how well agents are overseen, and how compute is allocated.
body: Anthropic said on Thursday it will publish three measurements intended to show the public how AI development is progressing inside the company. They cover how much of its AI research is carried out by AI, how well AI agents are supervised, and how its compute is allocated.
The company framed the disclosure as a response to systems being used to build their own successors. It published a snapshot of current values alongside the announcement.

The measures are self-reported. Anthropic defines each one, collects the underlying data and decides what to publish, so the figures describe what the company chooses to count rather than an externally verified position.

That said, the categories are the ones outside observers have asked about. A number for how much research is automated is a claim a company can be held to over time, which is more than most laboratories currently offer.
No other frontier laboratory publishes comparable figures, so there is nothing yet to compare them against.

stories.headline: Anthropic opens a verification programme for life science users
stories.standfirst: Verified professionals gain access to a wider range of biology work, including a model the company has not previously opened to it.
body: Anthropic has opened applications for what it calls a Life Sciences Verification Programme, under which professionals working in the life sciences can use its models with a different set of safeguards from the default.

The company said the programme gives access to models including Mythos, which it had not previously made available for this category of work. The stated aim is to let verified users carry out the full range of biology-related tasks.

The design acknowledges a problem the company has written about at length. Safeguards tuned to prevent misuse of biological capability also obstruct legitimate researchers, and a blanket restriction pushes real work elsewhere rather than making it safer.

Verification shifts that tradeoff rather than resolving it. Access now depends on Anthropic's assessment of who an applicant is, which concentrates the judgement inside the company rather than in the model's refusals.
The announcement is Anthropic's own. It has not published how applicants are assessed, how many have been approved, or what happens when a verified account is misused.

stories.headline: Claude optimised inference for thirty open biology models, Anthropic says
stories.standfirst: The company reports a fourfold speed-up and is funding a protein design competition to test more than five thousand designs experimentally.
body: Anthropic said Claude optimised inference for more than thirty open-source biology models, reporting speed-ups of around four times. The models covered tasks such as predicting molecular structure, designing drug-like molecules and assessing the effects of genetic mutations.

The stated problem is cost. Specialist biology models are expensive to run, which limits who can use them, and the company argues that making them cheaper widens access more than releasing another model would.

Alongside it, Anthropic is funding a protein design competition with Adaptyv Bio in which more than five thousand designs will be validated experimentally. It is providing up to $1 million in model credits plus funding, with Modal contributing compute and Twist Bioscience supplying DNA.

Experimental validation is the part that distinguishes this from a benchmark. A design that scores well computationally and fails at the bench has not worked, and competitions of this shape produce results that can be checked.
The speed-up figures are Anthropic's own, though the company published its code and a technical report alongside them, which makes the claim checkable in a way most are not.

stories.headline: Virginia creates an AI task force and a data centre accountability plan
stories.standfirst: Governor Spanberger's order cites workforce displacement, data privacy and cybersecurity, in the state carrying the largest concentration of data centres.
body: Governor Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday creating an artificial intelligence task force for Virginia, together with what her office describes as a data centre accountability plan.

The order cites workforce displacement, data privacy and cybersecurity as the concerns prompting it. Virginia carries the largest concentration of data centres in the United States, which makes the second element the more consequential of the two.

Data centre siting has become contested in the state over electricity demand, water use and the load new capacity places on the grid. An accountability plan implies reporting requirements, though the order does not yet set out what operators would have to disclose.

California moved the same day on a different question, with Governor Newsom ordering a study of a shutdown mechanism for frontier models. The two orders address opposite ends of the problem, one the physical build-out and the other the models themselves.
Neither imposes a binding requirement yet. Both are instructions to study and report, which is where state AI policy currently sits while federal rules remain unsettled.

sources.author: Office of the Governor of Virginia
